title: AI Agents Successfully Recreate the Gender Pay Gap
key_facts: Researchers at Ireland's University of Limerick published a study in which 189 knowledge workers worked with AI agents in a virtual-reality office.
Three agents performed identically: a text chatbot, a robotic-looking desk assistant, and a human-like one presented as male (“Johan”) or female (“Johanna”).
Workers rated each agent's work and allocated pay; human-like agents were rewarded more than the robotic one.
“Johan” was paid about 10% more on average than “Johanna” for the same performance and was seen as more human-like.
Of 34 people interviewed, 30 insisted they would treat the agents the same; only three acknowledged their behavior could reflect gender bias.
More participants said they felt more comfortable with female-presenting AI, which Gizmodo links to the female voices of Siri and Alexa.
quote_evidence: The study took 189 knowledge workers and placed them in a virtual reality office where they were made to work alongside three different AI agents to complete tasks.
The male “Johan” assistant was paid about 10% more on average than the female “Johanna” despite performing exactly the same—not too terribly far off the real-life gender pay gap.

Thirty of the 34 people interviewed insisted they would trust and reward an AI assistant the same, regardless of its gender presentation, while only three participants acknowledged that their behaviors could reflect gender bias.
why_it_matters_hint: Workplace gender bias appears to carry over to how people value AI helpers.
event_date: Study described as recently published; date and journal not stated; Gizmodo article 10 Oct 2026
notes: Full Gizmodo text read. Gizmodo names no journal and does not say whether the study was peer reviewed; the pay was allocated in a simulated task.
